transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-01
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (OmniHealth CTO), Maya Singh (Lead ML Eng), Evan Brooks (PM)

Summary: quick hosted API playthrough focusing on chat/text generation streaming behavior, parameter tradeoffs (temp/top-p/stream granularity), retry and idempotency strategies. Customer is evaluating hosted first, likely to move to dedicated if latency/cost require. Agreed to POC bench and share security docs.

Topics covered:
- API quickstart and Console tour
- Streaming semantics and partial responses vs finalization
- Token cost and latency tradeoffs (batching, kv cache)
- Retry patterns, idempotency keys, backoff strategies
- Sandbox POC plan and next steps

Action items (captured above)

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. Quick intros?
[00:12] Jordan: Jordan Lee, CTO at OmniHealth. We've got Maya and Evan with me.
[00:16] Maya: Hi all.
[00:18] Evan: Hi — thanks for the time.
[00:21] Alex: Great. Samira will run most of the demo, I'll chime on pricing and next steps. The goal for today is a hands-on playthrough of chat/text gen on the hosted API — streaming behavior, common params, and recommended retry patterns. We'll also show a bit of the Console and Optimize hints. Sound good?
[00:37] Jordan: Yep, perfect. We're evaluating for patient-facing summarization workflows, so latency matters but so does cost and data controls.
[00:46] Samira: Awesome. I'll share my screen — bringing up the quickstart. First, the REST call: conversation.create, you can stream by toggling stream=true. When streaming is on you get partial deltas which are flushed as tokens generate.
[01:07] Maya: Is the partial output guaranteed in-order? We've seen reordering in some earlier tests with other vendors.
[01:14] Samira: Good question. Streaming is ordered per-request; you may see chunking boundaries that split words, so clients should stitch fragments. We include sequence markers in the event stream but that depends on SDKs — the raw SSE delivers chunks in order.
[01:33] Alex: To add, if you need character-level flushes you can tune the stream granularity, but that will impact throughput vs small-chunk overhead.
[01:45] Evan: How does that impact cost? More frequent flushes means more tokens?
[01:50] Samira: Not directly tokens, but there is more RPC overhead and slightly higher latency for same throughput. Cost is per-token; overhead affects latency and throughput.
[02:05] Jordan: We care about tail latency for realtime UI. Typical SLO is p95 < 300ms for short prompts — is that realistic on hosted?
[02:15] Samira: For short prompts and smaller models, yes. We have verified p95 numbers in the Console; we can route by latency policy to lower-latency nodes. For multimodal or long-context workloads, p95 climbs — that's where Dedicated helps.
[02:34] Maya: Could you show batching/caching knobs? We run many similar prompts, prefix caching could help.
[02:41] Samira: Sure — in Optimize you get suggestions: enable prefix KV caching for repeated system prompts, and continuous batching with a max latency window, e.g., 20ms to aggregate requests.
[02:58] Alex: Note: KV cache is per-session and reduces compute for repeated context — we call it kv cache in the Console, sometimes folks spell it "K V cahce" in notes, ha.
[03:08] Maya: Ha, seen that. Is KV cache available on hosted or only dedicated?
[03:12] Samira: Hosted supports prefix/KV caching for common models; dedicated gives more control and longer retention windows.
[03:21] Evan: On retries — what's Redwood's recommended pattern? We saw a couple of transient 5xxs in earlier POC.
[03:28] Samira: We recommend client-side idempotency keys for non-streaming calls; for streaming, you should implement streaming resume: detect cut streams and either resume from last confirmed token or retry the last N tokens with overlap.
[03:44] Jordan: Any built-in dedupe? If the request persists and we accidentally re-send, we don't want duplicate actions.
[03:50] Samira: For generation calls, we treat them as side-effect-free by default; if you perform external side effects you should handle idempotency in your app. For server side we have request-IDs for logging and observability, but dedupe on the model output isn't automatic.
[04:06] Maya: Is there a recommended backoff schedule?
[04:09] Samira: Exponential backoff with jitter. For short retries we suggest 250ms base, *2 with jitter up to 1.5x, and cap at 5 seconds. Avoid aggressive retrying for model OOMs — we'll return explicit model error codes.
[04:24] Evan: Could you show a demo of a streaming session and a simulated network cut with resume?
[04:30] Samira: Yep, I'll fire a stream. (typing) Initiating stream... you can see partial tokens come in. Now I'll simulate a disconnect.
[04:46] [04:46] Samira: — (simulated) connection drop. Client sees last token '...cardio' confirmed at offset 24. Client can reconnect and request resume from offset 24 with idempotency key X.
[04:58] Maya: That resume API is part of the SDK?
[05:01] Samira: SDK supports it in the JS and Python libs; for raw REST you can pass resume_offset and original request-id. We also surface a 'finalized' event when the model indicates completion, so your client can differentiate between mid-stream disconnects and completed responses.
[05:21] Jordan: For our compliance folks, what logs/audit do you expose? Full transcripts?
[05:27] Alex: We provide per-request audit logs, token usage breakdowns, and request/response payloads in the Console. For hosted customers we retain logs per your retention policy; for regulated environments we recommend Private or Dedicated where you control retention and integrate with your KMS.
[05:45] Maya: Encryption at rest? KMS?
[05:47] Alex: Hosted encrypts at rest and in transit; we can integrate customer-managed KMS for Dedicated/Private.
[05:56] Evan: How about SSO and RBAC for multiple product teams?
[05:59] Alex: Console has SSO (SAML/OIDC), RBAC roles, and token scopes. We'll share the security whitepaper.
[06:10] Jordan: Great. Back to the demo — can you show param tuning: temperature/top_p/stop sequences?
[06:16] Samira: Sure. Here is a short prompt with temp=0.0 for deterministic output vs temp=0.8 to show diversity. Also Top-p has different behavior; use one or the other typically. You can fix max_new_tokens, presence penalty, etc.
[06:32] [06:32] Samira: (runs two requests) you can see deterministic completions vs more varied. Also, when streaming, small temp changes might alter token pacing which affects partial output arrival.
[06:47] Maya: What about truncation and context windows? We have clinical notes that can be 6k tokens. How to manage that?
[06:54] Samira: We support longer context models; for very long context we recommend summarization pipelines or retrieval-augmented generation with a vector store — Redwood handles embeddings too. There's also automatic context trimming policies.
[07:10] Evan: Do you have recommendations for cost control? We want predictable budget.
[07:13] Alex: Use Optimize suggestions: quantized models for cheaper throughput, token limits, response length caps, and routing lower-cost logical variants for non-critical requests. Also set alerts in Console for token usage spikes.
[07:29] Jordan: If we start hosted and then move to Dedicated, is the model/version compatibility seamless?
[07:34] Samira: Yes — same API surface. You can pin model versions and rollout policies. Fallbacks can route to hosted if dedicated capacity is exhausted, or vice versa.
[07:47] Maya: Could we do a quick latency benchmark using our sample prompts?
[07:51] Samira: We can run a quick smoke bench in the sandbox. If you share a prompt bank and target qps, we can run a 24–48 hour test and provide p50/p95/p99. That was part of the POC we discussed.
[08:04] Evan: Our traffic shape is spiky — around 200 rps bursts for short windows. How does autoscaling react?
[08:11] Alex: Dedicated autoscaling with burst capacity is configurable. Hosted elastic capacity is also designed to absorb spikes but with potential cold-warm handoff; you can configure router policy to favor dedicated when you need guaranteed SLOs.
[08:28] Jordan: Any quota limits on hosted for new customers? We may need a bump during POC.
[08:33] Alex: New accounts have soft limits; we can lift them for POC. We'll coordinate with support and infra.
[08:42] Maya: Can we see an example of how the Console surfaces streaming latency vs model compute time?
[08:48] Samira: (shares Console) here's the per-route breakdown: tokenization time, model compute, network transfer. You can filter by token position. Also Optimize will suggest lowering max_new_tokens if compute is dominating cost.
[09:06] Evan: About errors — what are common error codes and how to act on them?
[09:10] Samira: 429 for rate limits; 503/502 for infra transient; 400 for malformed inputs; 422 for safety checks. For 429s we recommend dynamic client-side throttling or queuing; for 5xx apply backoff and failover to a cheaper model or region.
[09:27] Jordan: Do you do automatic fallback between model families if a variant is out of capacity?
[09:32] Samira: Yes, smart routing can failover to compatible model variants using a policy you configure: strict (same model only), compatible (same family), or lowest-cost fallback.
[09:46] Maya: For health-care data, we need audit trails and ability to export logs to our SIEM. Is that possible?
[09:53] Alex: Yes, you can stream logs to your cloud storage or SIEM. For Private deployments you can keep everything on-prem. We'll include the export integration doc.
[10:05] Evan: Let's talk about streaming resume edge cases — if we resume mid-token, do we risk duplication or corruption?
[10:12] Samira: We resume at token boundaries. The client should track last confirmed token index from SSE events. If you can't confirm token boundary, conservative approach is to re-request last N tokens and dedupe by your own heuristics.
[10:27] Jordan: Could you demo a full quickstart from Console to API call and then the Optimize suggestion?
[10:33] Samira: Yep — creating a route in Console, set model, enable streaming, enable kv cache suggestion. Then run a test request. (typing) You can see Optimize flagged high variance in token lengths and suggests a max_tokens cap for higher predictability.
[10:56] Maya: In the Console, is there a way to pin model versions for canary rolling?
[11:00] Samira: Yes — rollouts allow canaries and percent traffic splits; you can set auto rollback on quality regressions measured by eval sets. We also support compare runs for A/B.
[11:15] Evan: For evals, do you integrate with our internal metric infra or is it Redwood-only?
[11:21] Alex: You can push eval results via API; Redwood also supports import of your evaluation harness.
[11:28] Jordan: How about security reviews — our procurement legal team will need SOC2 docs, pen test results, and data processing agreement.
[11:36] Alex: We'll send the SOC2 report, pen test summary, and our DPA template. For higher control the Private setup can be used.
[11:46] Maya: Is there an easy way to simulate spotty mobile networks? We want to replicate client disconnects.
[11:51] Samira: In the sandbox we have a network emulator; you can also simulate disconnects in the SDK directly. We'll share the test harness.
[12:04] Evan: One last thing — safety. We need to ensure model doesn't hallucinate PHI. Any guardrails?
[12:11] Samira: Redwood has content filters and safety policies; for PHI specifically we recommend prompt engineering and retrieval safeguards. We can run safety evals against your prompt set as part of the POC.
[12:28] Jordan: Ok that addresses most stuff. Let's move to schedule the POC.
[12:33] Alex: Proposed POC: 2 weeks, sandbox with 10k messages/day synthetic + your prompt set, perf bench with p95 targets, 1 security review run. Does that timeline fit?
[12:45] Maya: Yes, that's fine. We'll get the prompt bank over this week.
[12:49] Evan: We'll want a cost estimate for the POC and a lift for quotas.
[12:54] Alex: I'll send the cost spreadsheet and request a quota bump for the sandbox.
[12:58] Samira: I'll draft the bench plan and share test scripts.
[13:03] [13:03] Alex: Quick note — for long-term you might consider routing higher-value transactions to Dedicated with strict SLOs and leaving low-value background tasks on hosted to save cost.
[13:17] Jordan: Makes sense. Anything else?
[13:19] Maya: Could you include a sample resume handler in the SDK? That would be helpful.
[13:23] Samira: Yes, will attach the resume code snippet and a node/python example.
[13:29] Evan: And the SOC2 + DPA.
[13:32] Alex: On it.
[13:34] Jordan: Great, thanks.
[13:36] Alex: Thanks everyone — we'll recap and send next steps by EOD tomorrow.

(Conversation continues, troubleshooting a small Console permission issue, short cross-talk at ~22:00 about a specific tokenization quirk, then final recap)

[50:10] Alex: Recap — Alex to send pricing, SOC2, DPA; Samira to send sandbox runbook and bench scripts; Maya to send prompt bank. POC kickoff week of May 11.
[50:28] Jordan: Confirmed.
[50:30] Maya: Thanks all.
[50:32] Evan: Thanks.
[50:33] Samira: Thanks!
[50:35] Alex: Bye.
